concept_name: Why AB is the perpendicular bisector

item.question: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at O. Prove that O is the midpoint of XY and that AB is perpendicular to XY.
steps: In ΔABX and ΔABY: AX = AY, BX = BY, and AB is common. So ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by the SSS condition.
Corresponding parts are equal, so ∠XAB = ∠YAB, that is, ∠XAO = ∠YAO.
In ΔAOX and ΔAOY: AX = AY, ∠XAO = ∠YAO, and AO is common. So ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by the SAS condition.
Corresponding parts are equal, so OX = OY: O is the midpoint of XY.
Also ∠AOX = ∠AOY, and together they make a straight angle of 180°.
So each of ∠AOX and ∠AOY is half of 180°, which is 90°.
item.answer: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS; so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°: AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY
item.text:

2. Corresponding parts are equal, so ∠XAB = ∠YAB, that is, ∠XAO = ∠YAO.
3. In ΔAOX and ΔAOY: AX = AY, ∠XAO = ∠YAO, and AO is common. So ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by the SAS condition.
4. Corresponding parts are equal, so OX = OY: O is the midpoint of XY.
5. Also ∠AOX = ∠AOY, and together they make a straight angle of 180°.
6. So each of ∠AOX and ∠AOY is half of 180°, which is 90°.
Answer: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS; so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°: AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY

item.question: A point P is the same distance from X and Y, that is, PX = PY. Justify that P lies on the perpendicular bisector AB of XY.
steps_tex: If $P$ is on the same side of $XY$ as $A$, pair $P$ with $B$; otherwise pair $P$ with $A$. Say we pair $P$ with $B$.
Then $PX = PY$ and $BX = BY$, so $P$ and $B$ are each equally far from $X$ and $Y$.
In $\triangle PBX$ and $\triangle PBY$: $PX = PY$, $BX = BY$, and $PB$ is common, so $\triangle PBX$ is congruent to $\triangle PBY$ by $SSS$.

So $\angle XPB = \angle YPB$, and if $PB$ meets $XY$ at $O$, then $\triangle POX$ is congruent to $\triangle POY$ by $SAS$, with $PX = PY$, equal angles at $P$ and $PO$ common. So $OX = OY$ and the angles at $O$ are $90^\circ$.
So the line $PB$ is the perpendicular bisector of $XY$.
$XY$ has only one perpendicular bisector, the line $AB$, so $P$ lies on $AB$.

concept_name: Steps to construct the perpendicular bisector

item.question: Draw a line segment XY. Construct its perpendicular bisector using only an unmarked ruler and a compass, and mark the midpoint of XY.
steps: Open the compass to a radius more than half of XY, so that the arcs will meet.
With centre X, draw a long arc above XY. With centre Y and the same radius, draw an arc above XY that cuts it. Name the meeting point A.
Keep the same radius. With centres X and Y, draw two arcs below XY that cut each other at B.
Join A and B with the ruler. AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
Mark O where AB crosses XY. O is the midpoint of XY, and ∠AOX = 90°.
Reason: AX = AY and BX = BY, so ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS and then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS.
item.answer: AB, the line through the two meeting points of equal arcs, is the perpendicular bisector; it meets XY at its midpoint O
item.text:

3. Keep the same radius. With centres X and Y, draw two arcs below XY that cut each other at B.
4. Join A and B with the ruler. AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
5. Mark O where AB crosses XY. O is the midpoint of XY, and ∠AOX = 90°.
6. Reason: AX = AY and BX = BY, so ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS and then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS.

item.question: Draw a line and mark a point O on it. Construct a 90° angle at O using only a ruler and a compass, and say why the angle is 90°.
steps_tex: With centre $O$ and any radius, draw arcs that cut the line at $X$ and at $Y$. Then $OX = OY$.
Open the compass wider than $OX$. With centre $X$, draw an arc above the line.
With centre $Y$ and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at $A$. Then $AX = AY$.
Join $O$ and $A$. $\angle AOX$ is the required $90^\circ$ angle.
Reason: in $\triangle AOX$ and $\triangle AOY$, $AX = AY$, $OX = OY$, and $AO$ is common, so $\triangle AOX$ is congruent to $\triangle AOY$ by $SSS$.
So $\angle AOX = \angle AOY$. Together they make $180^\circ$, so each is $90^\circ$.
item.answer_tex: $\angle AOX = 90^\circ$, since $\triangle AOX$ is congruent to $\triangle AOY$ by $SSS$ and the two equal angles make a straight angle

item.question: Draw any angle ∠XOY. Bisect it using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the two parts are equal.
steps: With centre O and any radius, draw an arc that cuts OY at A and OX at B. Then OA = OB.
With centre A and a radius long enough for the arcs to meet, draw an arc inside the angle.
With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at C. Then AC = BC.
Join O and C.
In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common. So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS.
So ∠AOC = ∠BOC, and OC bisects ∠XOY.

4. Join O and C.
5. In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common. So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS.

steps_tex: Mark $A$ and $B$ on the arms with $OA = OB$.
With a radius larger than $OA$, draw equal arcs from $A$ and $B$ on the far side of $O$; they meet at $C$, with $AC = BC$.
In $\triangle OAC$ and $\triangle OBC$: $OA = OB$, $AC = BC$, and $OC$ is common.
So $\triangle OAC$ is congruent to $\triangle OBC$ by $SSS$, and $\angle AOC = \angle BOC$.
Extend $CO$ beyond $O$ to a point $D$ inside $\angle AOB$. $\angle AOD$ and $\angle AOC$ make a straight angle, and so do $\angle BOD$ and $\angle BOC$.
So $\angle AOD = 180^\circ - \angle AOC$ and $\angle BOD = 180^\circ - \angle BOC$; these are equal, so the line $CO$, extended beyond $O$, bisects $\angle AOB$.

item.question: What are the other angles that can be constructed using angle bisection? Can you construct 65.5° angle?
steps_tex: From $180^\circ$ by halving: $90^\circ$. From $90^\circ$ by halving: $45^\circ$, $22.5^\circ$, and so on.
Sums of these also work, for example $90^\circ + 45^\circ = 135^\circ$ and $45^\circ + 22.5^\circ = 67.5^\circ$.
Every angle made this way, doubled enough times, becomes a whole multiple of $45^\circ$.
$65.5^\circ$ doubled is $131^\circ$, and every further doubling is $131^\circ$ times a power of $2$, which is never a multiple of $45^\circ$, because $131$ is not divisible by $3$ or by $5$.
So $65.5^\circ$ cannot be constructed by bisection.

Later in this chapter we build a $60^\circ$ angle; halving it gives $30^\circ$ and $15^\circ$, and sums such as $75^\circ$. Those all double into multiples of $15^\circ$, and $131^\circ$ times a power of $2$ is not one of them either.
item.answer_tex: Angles such as $90^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $22.5^\circ$, $135^\circ$ and $67.5^\circ$ can be made (and, once $60^\circ$ is built, $30^\circ$, $15^\circ$ and $75^\circ$); $65.5^\circ$ cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of $45^\circ$, or even of $15^\circ$

steps_tex: Construct a square: a segment, right angles at both ends, equal sides cut with the compass, and join the fourth side.
Find the midpoint of each side by constructing its perpendicular bisector.
The two bisectors through opposite midpoints cross at the centre of the square.
With centre the midpoint of one side and radius half the side, draw a semicircle inside the square. It passes through the two corners at the ends of that side and through the centre.

steps_tex: With centre $A$ and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the two arms at $B$ and $C$. Then $AB = AC$.
Draw a ray from $X$. With centre $X$ and the same radius, draw a long arc that cuts the ray at $Z$. Then $XZ = AB$.
Open the compass to the length $BC$.
With centre $Z$ and radius $BC$, cut the arc at $Y$. Then $YZ = BC$ and $XY = AC$.
Join $X$ and $Y$.

item.question: A line m and a point B not on it are given. Construct a line through B parallel to m using only a ruler and a compass.
steps: Draw a line l through B that cuts m at A. l is the transversal.
With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts m at C and cuts l at D, on the part of l between A and B.
With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts l at F, on the side of B away from A, as for the matching corner.
Open the compass to CD. With centre F, cut the arc at E, on the same side of l as C.
Draw the line n through B and E. ΔBFE ≅ ΔADC by SSS, so the angle at B equals the angle at A.
These are corresponding angles, so n is parallel to m.
item.answer: The line n through B and E, since the copied corresponding angles are equal (SSS), so n ∥ m

4. Open the compass to CD. With centre F, cut the arc at E, on the same side of l as C.

6. These are corresponding angles, so n is parallel to m.

topic_name: A Regular Hexagon from Six Triangles
concept_name: Six equilateral triangles round a point

item.question: Six congruent equilateral triangles are placed round a centre O. Do they fit with no gap and no overlap, and is the outer figure a regular hexagon?
steps: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.
At O, six such angles meet, and 6 × 60 = 360, the complete angle round a point.
So the six triangles fit round O with no gap and no overlap.
The six outer sides are sides of congruent triangles, so they are all equal.
At each outer corner, two angles of 60° meet, making 120°. So all six angles are equal.
Equal sides and equal angles: the outer figure is a regular hexagon.
item.answer: Yes: six 60° angles make 360°, so they fit; the hexagon has equal sides and every angle is 120°
item.text:

3. So the six triangles fit round O with no gap and no overlap.
4. The six outer sides are sides of congruent triangles, so they are all equal.
